title: Beyond Tikka Masala: Kerala's Coconut-and-Curry-Leaf Cuisine Stakes Its Claim in America
excerpt: Datassential named Keralan food a 'Cuisine to Know for 2026' as coconut-forward South Indian restaurants multiply across major U.S. metros.
body:
For decades, "Indian food" in America meant a familiar shorthand: butter chicken, naan and a dim buffet steam table. That ceiling is finally cracking, and the wedge driving through it tastes of coconut milk, curry leaves and the faint, funky perfume of asafoetida. Keralan cuisine — the seafood-rich, vegetable-forward cooking of India's southwestern coast — has been named a "Cuisine to Know for 2026" by the food-intelligence platform Datassential, and a wave of restaurants is racing to prove the label right.

## Context & Background

Kerala sits on the Malabar Coast, where centuries of spice trade with Arab, Portuguese and Chinese merchants layered new techniques onto a thousand-year-old cooking tradition. The result is a cuisine that looks almost nothing like the cream-heavy North Indian fare most Americans first encountered. Coconut appears in nearly every form — grated, as milk, as oil. Rice takes the place of wheat breads. Dishes lean lighter, brighter and often vegetarian, anchored by spices such as curry leaves, turmeric and the pungent asafoetida that Datassential singled out in its trends report. According to that research, 39% of U.S. consumers say they are interested in trying Keralan food — a strikingly high number for a regional cuisine most could not have named a year ago.

The appetite is part of a broader rebalancing. As one Datassential-cited analysis put it, diners are moving past "broad categories" toward the depth of India's regional kitchens, with Goan, Naga and Himalayan cooking queued up behind Kerala's breakout.

## Current Developments

The clearest signal is on the ground in New York. Chatti, a Manhattan restaurant from chef Regi Mathew, has drawn praise for being rooted "entirely in the state of Kerala's cooking heritage" rather than serving a pan-Indian greatest-hits menu. "Even as NYC is experiencing a surge of regional Indian cuisine," noted wellness chef Dalia David after dining there, Chatti stands out because Keralan food is "vibrant, vegetable-forward, and rooted in grated coconut — not drowned in heavy, dairy cream-based sauces."

Nearby in the East Village, chef Aarthi Sampath's new restaurant Drāvida widens the lens to the whole South Asian diaspora, tracing how South Indian flavors traveled to the Caribbean, Africa and Southeast Asia. Its menu runs from Trinidadian doubles to an idli-and-shrimp dish inspired by South Indian and Indonesian cooking — proof that the regional turn is also a diaspora story.

The momentum extends well beyond restaurants with celebrity chefs. Industry trackers report supper clubs and pop-ups built around single regional menus, and Yelp search data shows surging interest in newly opened, regionally specific concepts.

## Diaspora Impact

For Malayali families abroad, the shift carries unusual emotional weight. Appam and stew, puttu, Kerala fish curry and the grand vegetarian sadya served on a banana leaf have long been cooked at home and rarely found on American menus worth recommending to non-Indian friends. Seeing them plated at a buzzed-about Manhattan opening is a quiet vindication — the food of a specific place, eaten with pride rather than apology.

It also reframes the conversation second-generation NRIs have been having for years. Indian food is not a monolith, and the arrival of restaurants that say so out loud gives diaspora diners a way to share the cuisine of their grandmother's kitchen, not a generic stand-in.

## What's Next

The open question is whether Kerala's moment becomes a foundation or a fad. Restaurateurs are betting it sticks, with regional concepts multiplying across major metros and investors circling modern-Indian dining. Datassential's forecasters expect Goa, Nagaland and the Himalayan thali to follow Kerala into the spotlight, each carrying its own argument that India contains as many cuisines as a continent. For now, the curry leaf is having its turn — and for a generation of diaspora cooks, it tastes a lot like home.
